## Overview

Backpressure is a mechanism in streaming and reactive systems where a slow downstream consumer signals to an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate. Without backpressure, an unbounded buffer between producer and consumer will grow until the process runs out of memory, leading to system failure.

## Problem

In a typical producer-consumer pipeline, the producer may emit data faster than the consumer can process it. Without a feedback mechanism, intermediate buffers grow without bound, consuming all available memory. This is particularly acute in:

- High-throughput data streams
- Network systems with variable latency
- Real-time processing pipelines
- Reactive and async systems

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queue with Blocking

The producer writes to a fixed-size queue. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer thread blocks until the consumer drains some items, freeing buffer space. This is straightforward but can lead to context switching overhead.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

The consumer explicitly grants the producer a "credit" — permission to send N more items. Once the producer exhausts its credit, it stops emitting until the consumer issues new credit. This approach decouples producer and consumer timing and is common in protocols like QUIC and various message brokers.

### Reactive Pull Model

Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. The producer only emits when asked. This inverts control flow and naturally prevents overproduction.
